body_ar:
من الأركان التي يجب على كل مسلم الإيمان بها: الإيمان بالكتب التي أنزلها الله عز وجل على رسله وأنبيائه، ما سمي منها وما لم يسم، وأن القرآن خاتمها وناسخها، وأنه كلام الله عز وجل. ومما يجب الإيمان به أن كلام الله عز وجل صفة من صفاته، فهو يتكلم متى شاء بما شاء، بصوت وحرف لا يشبهه في ذلك أحد من خلقه.
وجوب الإيمان بالكتب المنزلة من عند الله عز وجل:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين، وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين، وعلى آله وأصحابه أجمعين. سبحانك اللهم لا علم لنا إلا ما علمتنا إنك أنت العليم الحكيم، اللهم علمنا ما ينفعنا، وانفعنا بما علمتنا، وزدنا علماً يا أرحم الراحمين! يقول الشيخ حفظه الله: [والكتب التي على رسل البشر أنزل من كلامه جل فذر قولهم القرآن قد دل على الـ كلام أو على الذي الكلام دل] من أركان الإيمان: الإيمان بالكتب المنزلة، وهذا الركن في أصله داخل في الركن الأول الذي هو الإيمان بالله؛ فأركان الإيمان ستة، لكن ثلاثة منها ترجع إلى واحد. فالإيمان بالله يشمل الإيمان بالكتب المنزلة والإيمان بالقدر؛ لأن الكتب المنزلة كلام الله، والقدر من علم الله، فهذا كله يرجع إلى الإيمان بالله. فإذاً: تعود هذه الأقسام في حقيقتها إلى أربعة: الإيمان بالله، والإيمان بالملائكة، والإيمان بالرسل، والإيمان باليوم الآخر...
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* Among the pillars that every Muslim is obliged to believe in is belief in the Books that God, mighty and majestic, sent down upon His messengers and His prophets — those of them that are named and those that are not — and that the Qur'an is the seal of them and abrogates them, and that it is the speech of God, mighty and majestic. And of what must be believed is that the speech of God, mighty and majestic, is one of His attributes: He speaks when He wills, with what He wills, with voice and letter, in which no one of His creation resembles Him.

## The obligation (wājib) to believe in the Books sent down from God, mighty and majestic

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of mercy. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. I invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions all together. *Glory be to You, O God; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us; indeed You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. O God, teach us what benefits us, and benefit us by what You have taught us, and increase us in knowledge, O Most Merciful of those who show mercy!*

The Sheikh, may God preserve him, says:

*[And the Books that were sent down upon the messengers of mankind are of His speech, majestic is He — so leave aside their saying that the Qur'an points to the speech, or points to that which the speech points to.]*

Among the pillars of faith is belief in the revealed Books. This pillar, at root, falls within the first pillar, which is belief in God. The pillars of faith are six, but three of them go back to one. For belief in God comprises belief in the revealed Books and belief in the decree, because the revealed Books are the speech of God, and the decree belongs to God's knowledge; so all of this goes back to belief in God.

Thus these divisions come back, in reality, to four: belief in God, belief in the angels, belief in the messengers, and belief in the Last Day…

flags.note: Excerpt only, style guide section 9. The full lesson sits behind /medias/doc/esmawesivat-12.doc. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends and completes nothing. Must not be rendered as a whole lesson.

flags.arabic: الفقرة الافتتاحية مقابل ما بعد العنوان الفرعي
flags.context: the synopsis paragraph against the transcribed commentary
options: mark the synopsis as the site's own and the remainder as the Sheikh's words
present the whole record as the Sheikh's words
flags.note: The record has more than one author. The opening paragraph is a synopsis written by the site, speaking about the lesson in the third person; everything from the section heading onward is the lecturer's own words as transcribed, together with the quoted line of the versified base text, which is his teacher's. The site must keep the voices apart.

flags.context: فهو يتكلم متى شاء بما شاء، بصوت وحرف لا يشبهه في ذلك أحد من خلقه
options: in an audible and articulated manner
flags.note: Style guide section 12. This is a contested creedal formulation: the affirmation of divine speech 'with voice and letter' is the Hanbali and Athari position and is explicitly rejected by the Ashʿaris and Maturidis, whose doctrine of inner speech (al-kalām al-nafsī) the quoted line of verse then tells the student to set aside. In English on a standalone page it reads as a ruling against two of the three surviving Sunni creedal schools. Translated exactly; no softening, and no gloss added. Note also that this sentence is the site's synopsis, not the Sheikh's transcribed words, which makes attributing it to him doubly a matter for his office.

flags.arabic: فذر قولهم القرآن قد دل على الكلام أو على الذي الكلام دل
flags.context: the quoted line of the versified base text
options: so leave aside their saying that the Qur'an points to the speech, or points to that which the speech points to
so reject their claim that the Qur'an indicates the speech, or indicates what the speech indicates
flags.note: The referent of 'their' is not named in the excerpt and the Sheikh does not gloss it before the record stops. In the literature this line is directed at the Ashʿari doctrine that the recited Qur'an indicates God's eternal inner speech rather than being it. The English keeps the pronoun unresolved exactly as the Arabic does; the identification must come from the Sheikh's office or from the .doc, not from the translator.

flags.context: فالإيمان بالله يشمل الإيمان بالكتب المنزلة والإيمان بالقدر
flags.note: Style guide section 13 lists qaḍāʾ/qadar as a pending glossary addition and instructs workers to flag rather than assume. The flattest rendering is used here and the term is left for the glossary decision. Note that the existing glossary entry for qaḍāʾ ('judicial ruling' / 'making up a missed act of worship') covers neither sense in play in this sentence.

translator_notes: One of a run of fourteen records, IDs 734-747, the series 'The Names and Attributes', all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/esmawesivat-* series, numbered 1 to 14 in the same order as the IDs.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.

This record does carry a CMS timestamp in a .create_date span (10 May 2011, within a 28-minute window shared by the whole run 738-747). That is a bulk-upload timestamp for the series, not the date the lesson was given. Record 737, translated in an earlier wave, reports no date for this run; the timestamp is in fact present in the page and should be backfilled there.

Creedal material. Per style guide section 8, the vocabulary of divine attributes is not the vocabulary of the five legal rulings, and the five-rulings mapping is not applied to any predicate of God in this record.

This record differs from the rest of the run in opening with the khuṭbat al-ḥājah and the teaching supplication, which places it at the start of a session rather than mid-series. The supplication is given in English with the Arabic retained in the facing pane, per style guide section 4, since it is recited text.

'يجب على كل مسلم الإيمان' is a ruling on a human act and is rendered 'is obliged to believe' / 'the obligation (wājib)' under style guide section 3. The kalām exemption of section 8 does not reach it. The predicates of God elsewhere in the record are handled under section 8 and are not given legal renderings.
The arithmetic of the passage is sound and is not a source defect: six pillars, of which belief in God, in the Books and in the decree are the three that collapse into one, leaving four.

Marked critical_for_display: the excerpt stops immediately after reducing the pillars to four, with no treatment of the revealed Books themselves — the announced subject of the lesson — and with the polemical line of verse left standing as the last substantive claim on the page.
